text: When Ivan Ivanych visited his brother for the first time, the place was hot and cheerless, crowded with fences, ditches, and rows of young fir trees. <break time="0.8s" /> A fat reddish dog that looked rather like a pig tried to bark but was too lazy, and a barefoot cook, also fat and piglike, said her master was resting. <break time="0.8s" /> Nikolai himself lay in bed, grown stout and flabby, with his cheeks, nose, and lips pushed forward so that he seemed about to grunt into the quilt. <break time="0.8s" /> Nikolai had changed completely, for the shy, timid clerk of earlier years now behaved like a grand gentleman and was deeply offended when the peasants failed to call him Your Honor. <break time="0.8s" /> He spoke solemnly, like a government minister, about education and the common people, treated sick peasants with simple medicines, and served them vodka on his name day. <break time="0.8s" /> Nikolai now spoke of himself proudly as a nobleman, even though their grandfather had been a peasant and their father a soldier who had risen to the rank of officer. <break time="0.8s" /> That evening the cook brought in a plate of gooseberries, the very first picked from the bushes, and Nikolai looked at them in silence, with tears in his eyes. <break time="0.8s" /> Then he put one berry in his mouth and, with the triumph of a child who has finally been given a long promised toy, exclaimed, How delicious. <break time="0.8s" /> Yet the gooseberries were hard and sour, and Ivan Ivanych realized that his brother, deceiving himself with a pleasant illusion, was happier than any truth could make him.
